    // Mobile navigation behavior: animated hamburger, slide-in drawer, overlay, and focus trap
    (function () {
      const hamburger = document.getElementById('hamburger');
      const mobileNav = document.getElementById('mobile-nav');
      const overlay = document.getElementById('overlay');
      let focusableEls = [];
      let firstFocusable = null;
      let lastFocusable = null;
      let lastActiveElement = null;

      function updateFocusable() {
        focusableEls = mobileNav.querySelectorAll('a[href], button, textarea, input, select, [tabindex]:not([tabindex="-1"])');
        firstFocusable = focusableEls[0];
        lastFocusable = focusableEls[focusableEls.length - 1];
      }

      function trapTabKey(e) {
        if (e.key !== 'Tab') return;
        if (focusableEls.length === 0) {
          e.preventDefault();
          return;
        }
        if (e.shiftKey) {
          // Shift + Tab
          if (document.activeElement === firstFocusable) {
            e.preventDefault();
            lastFocusable.focus();
          }
        } else {
          // Tab
          if (document.activeElement === lastFocusable) {
            e.preventDefault();
            firstFocusable.focus();
          }
        }
      }

      function openNav() {
        document.body.classList.add('nav-open');
        hamburger.setAttribute('aria-expanded', 'true');
        overlay.style.display = 'block';
        updateFocusable();
        // Focus the first item for accessibility
        if (firstFocusable) firstFocusable.focus();
        lastActiveElement = document.activeElement;
        document.addEventListener('keydown', trapTabKey);
      }

      function closeNav() {
        document.body.classList.remove('nav-open');
        hamburger.setAttribute('aria-expanded', 'false');
        overlay.style.display = 'none';
        document.removeEventListener('keydown', trapTabKey);
        // Restore focus to the button that opened the menu
        if (typeof lastActiveElement !== 'undefined' && lastActiveElement) {
          lastActiveElement.focus();
        } else {
          hamburger.focus();
        }
      }

      // Open/close handlers
      hamburger.addEventListener('click', function () {
        const isOpen = document.body.classList.contains('nav-open');
        if (isOpen) {
          closeNav();
        } else {
          lastActiveElement = document.activeElement;
          openNav();
        }
      });

      overlay.addEventListener('click', closeNav);

      // Close on Escape
      document.addEventListener('keydown', function (e) {
        if (e.key === 'Escape' && document.body.classList.contains('nav-open')) {
          closeNav();
        }
      });

      // Initialize overlay display state
      overlay.style.display = 'none';
    })();
  </script>
</body>
</html>

Notes and customization tips:
- The hamburger morphs to an X via transforms on the three bars when the menu is open.
- The navigation drawer slides in from the left; an overlay darkens the rest of the page and closes the menu when clicked.
- Accessibility: aria-expanded on the button, proper nav role, focus moves to the first item when opened, and focus trap keeps focus within the drawer until it’s closed. Escape closes the menu and restores focus to the hamburger button.
- You can adapt the widths, colors, and breakpoints in CSS to fit your design.

  <script>
    // Enable click-to-toggle for dropdowns on all devices
    document.addEventListener('DOMContentLoaded', function() {
      const toggles = document.querySelectorAll('.dropdown-toggle');
      toggles.forEach(btn => {
        btn.addEventListener('click', function(e) {
          // Toggle this dropdown
          const parent = this.closest('.has-dropdown');
          const isOpen = parent.classList.toggle('open');
          this.setAttribute('aria-expanded', String(isOpen));

          // Close any other open dropdowns
          document.querySelectorAll('.has-dropdown').forEach(item => {
            if (item !== parent) {
              item.classList.remove('open');
              const otherBtn = item.querySelector('.dropdown-toggle');
              if (otherBtn) otherBtn.setAttribute('aria-expanded', 'false');
            }
          });
        });
      });

      // Close dropdowns when clicking outside the nav
      document.addEventListener('mousedown', function(e) {
        const isInside = e.target.closest('.main-nav');
        if (!isInside) {
          document.querySelectorAll('.has-dropdown.open').forEach(item => {
            item.classList.remove('open');
            const b = item.querySelector('.dropdown-toggle');
            if (b) b.setAttribute('aria-expanded', 'false');
          });
        }
      });

      // Close with Escape key
      document.addEventListener('keydown', function(e) {
        if (e.key === 'Escape') {
          document.querySelectorAll('.has-dropdown.open').forEach(item => {
            item.classList.remove('open');
            const b = item.querySelector('.dropdown-toggle');
            if (b) b.setAttribute('aria-expanded', 'false');
          });
        }
      });
    });
  </script>
</body>
</html>

The nature of consciousness and whether it can exist independently of a physical body are hotly debated in philosophy, cognitive science, and even some spiritual traditions. Here’s a concise overview of the main positions and what they imply about independence from physical form.

What is consciousness?
- Broadly: the subjective experience of being aware—feelings, sensations, thoughts, intentions, and the sense of a first-person perspective.
- The big puzzle (the “hard problem”): why and how physical processes in the brain give rise to subjective experience at all.

Major positions in the philosophy of mind
- Physicalism / Materialism
  - Claim: consciousness is nothing over and above brain Activity; mental states are brain states or tightly dependent on them.
  - Subtypes: reductive (every mental state maps directly to a brain state) and non-reductive (mental properties depend on but are not reducible to brain states).
  - Implication for independence: generally says consciousness cannot exist without some physical substrate (like a brain or a sufficiently complex system).

- Emergentism
  - Claim: consciousness emerges from complex interactions of non-conscious components (e.g., neurons) but is not reducible to any one part.
  - Implication: still requires a physical substrate; not independently existing apart from it in any ordinary sense.

- Functionalism
  - Claim: mental states are defined by their functional roles (inputs, outputs, and causal relationships) rather than their material makeup.
  - Implication: could, in principle, exist in non-biological systems (e.g., machines) as long as the right functional organization is present. Does not by itself claim disembodied consciousness.

- Dualism (including substance dualism)
  - Claim: mind and body are distinct substances; consciousness can exist independently of physical form.
  - Interaction problem: how does a non-physical mind interact with a physical brain? What counts as evidence of disembodied consciousness?
  - Implication for independence: traditionally allows for persistence of consciousness without a physical body (though it faces serious explanatory challenges).

- Property dualism
  - Claim: physical things have both physical properties and non-physical (mental) properties; consciousness arises as a set of non-physical properties supervening on physical states.
  - Implication for independence: does not strictly require a separate mind/substance, but still posits non-physical aspects.

- Panpsychism / Neutral monism
  - Panpsychism: consciousness (or proto-consciousness) is a fundamental property of matter; even elementary parts have some basic experiential aspect.
  - Neutral monism: reality has one underlying substance that is neither purely mental nor purely physical; consciousness and the physical world are different manifestations of the same underlying reality.
  - Implication for independence: these views often treat consciousness as pervasive or intrinsic to reality, not something that only appears inside a particular brain.

- Idealism
  - Claim: reality at bottom is mental; the “physical” world arises from conscious experience.
  - Implication for independence: if correct, consciousness is more fundamental than any supposed physical form.

Empirical considerations
- Neuroscience has mapped correlations between brain activity and conscious states, but these correlations do not yet prove how subjective experience arises.
- The “hard problem” remains: explaining why brain processes are accompanied by experience rather than by objective, third-person information alone.
- Some researchers favor interpretations like information processing or predictive coding that try to explain function without invoking non-physical substances.
- Anecdotes like near-death experiences or out-of-body experiences are reported, but they do not provide widely accepted, reproducible evidence for disembodied consciousness.

Can consciousness exist independently of physical form?
- If you adopt physicalism or emergentist views: typically no. Consciousness is grounded in physical substrates (brains, or sufficiently complex systems).
- If you adopt dualism, panpsychism, neutral monism, or idealism: yes, in some formulations. For example, a non-physical mind that persists after bodily death; or consciousness as a fundamental aspect of reality.
- The strongest scientific stance today: there is no conclusive evidence for disembodied consciousness, and the best-supported views tie consciousness closely to physical processes. However, many philosophers and some scientists argue that the question is still open at a fundamental level.

Key ideas
- Psychological egoism (descriptive): all human actions are ultimately motivated by self-interest, even when we appear to help others.
- Altruism (genuine selflessness): acting to help others with no expectation of personal gain, even at a cost to oneself.
- Mixed motives: many actions involve both concern for others and self-related goals (happiness, avoidance of guilt, social approval, future reciprocity).

What the evidence and arguments suggest
- Empirical findings:
  - Prosocial behavior often involves a “warm glow” or reward feeling in the brain when helping others, which can suggest self-benefit as part of the motivation.
  - People frequently help in ways that also benefit themselves (e.g., improving mood, gaining social status, avoiding guilt, or increasing future reciprocity). This is compatible with a mix of motives rather than pure selflessness.

- Biological and evolutionary perspectives:
  - Kin selection and reciprocal altruism explain why individuals act to help others: helping relatives or cooperating in a group can improve one’s own genetic lineage or long-term survival, which is a form of self-interest at the level of genes or evolutionary fitness.
  - These explanations don’t deny genuine care or moral motivation, but they show that apparent selflessness often has roots in self-preservation at a broader level.
- Philosophical perspectives:
  - Kantian ethics: some actions are morally good because they are done from duty, not from self-interest, even if they have no personal payoff.
  - Utilitarianism: the right action is the one that maximizes overall welfare, which can require self-sacrifice for greater good.
  - Virtue ethics: a virtuous person acts from a stable character that values others for their own sake, not merely to achieve personal gain; such actions can feel genuinely selfless to the actor.

What counts as “genuine selflessness”
- A useful way to think about it is whether the motive is to benefit the other for their sake, with no expectation of any personal benefit (not even a feeling of moral satisfaction, or not knowingly seeking future rewards).
- In practice, even acts that feel selfless to the recipient can have implicit self-benefits for the actor (self-respect, social standing, future reciprocity). That doesn’t invalidate the action, but it does complicate the claim of pure selflessness.

Practical implications
- If you’re trying to cultivate selflessness, focusing on empathy, perspective-taking, and values-based living can help align actions with others’ welfare.
- Societal structures can encourage genuine altruism by reducing the salience of personal gain (anonymous giving, charitable norms, transparency about costs and benefits, reputational safeguards that reward compassionate acts without ulterior motives).
- It’s realistic to recognize that motives are often mixed. This doesn’t negate the positive impact of helping others; it just reframes the question of “why” we help.

Bottom line
Humans can perform genuinely selfless acts, but many actions are influenced by self-interest in various ways. The most defensible stance is nuanced: self-interest and altruistic concern often coexist, sometimes with one motive dominant and other times with motives that are hard to separate. Whether an action is truly selfless may depend on how precisely we define motivation and how thoroughly we can rule out any personal benefit.

Here's a minimal 3-layer neural network implemented from scratch without libraries. The code trains on the XOR dataset over 10,000 epochs, printing progress every 1,000 epochs.

```python
import random
import math

class NeuralNetwork:
    def __init__(self, input_size, hidden_size, output_size, seed=None):
        if seed is not None:
            random.seed(seed)
        self.input_size = input_size
        self.hidden_size = hidden_size
        self.output_size = output_size
        
        # Initialize weights and biases
        self.W1 = [[random.uniform(-1.0, 1.0) for _ in range(input_size)] for _ in range(hidden_size)]
        self.b1 = [random.uniform(-1.0, 1.0) for _ in range(hidden_size)]
        self.W2 = [[random.uniform(-1.0, 1.0) for _ in range(hidden_size)] for _ in range(output_size)]
        self.b2 = [random.uniform(-1.0, 1.0) for _ in range(output_size)]

    def sigmoid(self, z):
        return 1.0 / (1.0 + math.exp(-z))

    def sigmoid_prime(self, z):
        s = self.sigmoid(z)
        return s * (1 - s)

    def forward(self, x):
        Z1 = [sum(self.W1[i][j] * x[j] for j in range(self.input_size)) + self.b1[i] for i in range(self.hidden_size)]
        A1 = [self.sigmoid(z) for z in Z1]
        Z2 = [sum(self.W2[i][j] * A1[j] for j in range(self.hidden_size)) + self.b2[i] for i in range(self.output_size)]
        A2 = [self.sigmoid(z) for z in Z2]
        return A1, A2, Z1, Z2

    def train(self, X, Y, epochs=10000, lr=0.5, verbose=False):
        for epoch in range(epochs):
            err = 0.0
            for x, y in zip(X, Y):
                y_vec = [y]
                A1, A2, Z1, Z2 = self.forward(x)
                delta2 = [(A2[i] - y_vec[i]) * self.sigmoid_prime(Z2[i]) for i in range(self.output_size)]
                delta1 = []
                for j in range(self.hidden_size):
                    d = sum(self.W2[i][j] * delta2[i] for i in range(self.output_size))
                    delta1.append(d * self.sigmoid_prime(Z1[j]))
                for i in range(self.output_size):
                    for j in range(self.hidden_size):
                        grad = delta2[i] * A1[j]
                        self.W2[i][j] -= lr * grad
                    self.b2[i] -= lr * delta2[i]
                for i in range(self.hidden_size):
                    for j in range(self.input_size):
                        grad = delta1[i] * x[j]
                        self.W1[i][j] -= lr * grad
                    self.b1[i] -= lr * delta1[i]
                err += 0.5 * sum((A2[i] - y_vec[i])**2 for i in range(self.output_size))
            if verbose and (epoch % max(1, epochs//10) == 0 or epoch == epochs-1):
                print(f"Epoch {epoch}, error={err}")

    def predict(self, x):
        _, A2, _, _ = self.forward(x)
        return A2[0]

def main():
    X = [[0, 0], [0, 1], [1, 0], [1, 1]]
    Y = [0, 1, 1, 0]

    nn = NeuralNetwork(input_size=2, hidden_size=2, output_size=1, seed=42)
    nn.train(X, Y, epochs=10000, lr=0.5, verbose=True)

    for x in X:
        out = nn.predict(x)
        print(f"input={x}, output={out:.4f}, binary={1 if out >= 0.5 else 0}")

if __name__ == '__main__':
    main()
```</think> Here's a minimal 3-layer (2-2-1) neural network implemented from scratch in Python without using any libraries. It includes forward pass, backpropagation, and training on the XOR problem.

```python
import random
import math

class NeuralNetwork:
    def __init__(self, input_size, hidden_size, output_size, seed=None):
        if seed is not None:
            random.seed(seed)

        self.input_size = input_size
        self.hidden_size = hidden_size
        self.output_size = output_size

        # Initialize weights and biases with small random values
        self.W1 = [[random.uniform(-1.0, 1.0) for _ in range(input_size)]
                   for _ in range(hidden_size)]   # hidden_size x input_size
        self.b1 = [random.uniform(-1.0, 1.0) for _ in range(hidden_size)]  # hidden_size

        self.W2 = [[random.uniform(-1.0, 1.0) for _ in range(hidden_size)]
                   for _ in range(output_size)]  # output_size x hidden_size
        self.b2 = [random.uniform(-1.0, 1.0) for _ in range(output_size)]  # output_size

    def sigmoid(self, z):
        return 1.0 / (1.0 + math.exp(-z))

    def sigmoid_prime(self, z):
        s = self.sigmoid(z)
        return s * (1.0 - s)

    def forward(self, x):
        # x: list of length input_size
        Z1 = [sum(self.W1[i][j] * x[j] for j in range(self.input_size)) + self.b1[i]
              for i in range(self.hidden_size)]
        A1 = [self.sigmoid(z) for z in Z1]

        Z2 = [sum(self.W2[i][j] * A1[j] for j in range(self.hidden_size)) + self.b2[i]
              for i in range(self.output_size)]
        A2 = [self.sigmoid(z) for z in Z2]

        return A1, A2, Z1, Z2

    def train(self, X, Y, epochs=10000, lr=0.5, verbose=False):
        # X: list of input vectors
        # Y: list of targets (0 or 1)
        for epoch in range(epochs):
            err = 0.0
            for x, y in zip(X, Y):
                y_vec = [y]  # make it a list for consistency
                A1, A2, Z1, Z2 = self.forward(x)

                # Output layer error
                delta2 = [(A2[i] - y_vec[i]) * self.sigmoid_prime(Z2[i])
                          for i in range(self.output_size)]

                # Backpropagate to the hidden layer
                delta1 = []
                for j in range(self.hidden_size):
                    d = sum(self.W2[i][j] * delta2[i] for i in range(self.output_size))
                    delta1.append(d * self.sigmoid_prime(Z1[j]))

                # Update W2 and b2
                for i in range(self.output_size):
                    for j in range(self.hidden_size):
                        grad = delta2[i] * A1[j]
                        self.W2[i][j] -= lr * grad
                    self.b2[i] -= lr * delta2[i]

                # Update W1 and b1
                for i in range(self.hidden_size):
                    for j in range(self.input_size):
                        grad = delta1[i] * x[j]
                        self.W1[i][j] -= lr * grad
                    self.b1[i] -= lr * delta1[i]

                # Accumulate squared error
                err += 0.5 * sum((A2[i] - y_vec[i])**2 for i in range(self.output_size))

            if verbose and (epoch % max(1, epochs // 10) == 0 or epoch == epochs - 1):
                print(f"Epoch {epoch}, error={err:.6f}")

    def predict(self, x):
        _, A2, _, _ = self.forward(x)
        return A2[0]

def main():
    # XOR problem
    X = [
        [0, 0],
        [0, 1],
        [1, 0],
        [1, 1]
    ]
    Y = [0, 1, 1, 0]

    nn = NeuralNetwork(input_size=2, hidden_size=2, output_size=1, seed=42)
    nn.train(X, Y, epochs=10000, lr=0.5, verbose=True)

    print("Predictions after training:")
    for x in X:
        out = nn.predict(x)
        print(f"Input: {x}, Output: {out:.4f}, Class: {1 if out >= 0.5 else 0}")

if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()
```

Notes:
- This is a simple 2-2-1 feedforward network trained with backpropagation on the XOR task.
- No external libraries are used; all math is done with Python lists and standard library.
- You can adjust the architecture by changing input_size, hidden_size, and output_size, or try other tasks by changing X and Y.

#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""
Sentiment analysis for social media posts using NLP techniques.

Two approaches are provided:
  1) VADER (NLTK) - fast, good for short, informal text common to social media.
  2) Transformer-based (HuggingFace) - more nuanced, but heavier to load.

Usage:
  - Install required packages:
      pip install pandas nltk transformers torch

  - Run this script as-is (VADER will be used by default).
  - To try the transformer method, set method='transformer' when constructing the analyzer.
"""

import re
import pandas as pd
from typing import List, Dict, Optional

# Attempt to set up VADER (NLTK)
_USE_VADER = False
try:
    import nltk
    from nltk.sentiment import SentimentIntensityAnalyzer
    nltk.download('vader_lexicon', quiet=True)
    _VADER_ANALYZER = SentimentIntensityAnalyzer()
    _USE_VADER = True
except Exception:
    _VADER_ANALYZER = None

# Attempt to set up a Transformer-based sentiment model
_USE_TRANSFORMERS = False
_TRANSFORMER_PIPELINE = None
try:
    from transformers import pipeline
    # Use a SST-2 fine-tuned model (POS/NEG)
    _TRANSFORMER_PIPELINE = pipeline("sentiment-analysis", model="distilbert-base-uncased-finetuned-sst-2-english")
    _USE_TRANSFORMERS = True
except Exception:
    _TRANSFORMER_PIPELINE = None

class SentimentAnalyzer:
    """
    Simple sentiment analyzer over posts using:
      - 'vader' : NLTK VADER
      - 'transformer' : HuggingFace SST-2 fine-tuned model
    """
    def __init__(self, method: str = "vader"):
        method = method.lower()
        if method not in ("vader", "transformer"):
            raise ValueError("method must be 'vader' or 'transformer'")

        self.method = method
        if method == "vader":
            if not _USE_VADER:
                raise RuntimeError("VADER is not available (NLTK download may have failed).")
            self.analyzer = _VADER_ANALYZER
        else:  # transformer
            if not _USE_TRANSFORMERS:
                raise RuntimeError("Transformer pipeline is not available. Install transformers and a compatible model.")
            self.pipeline = _TRANSFORMER_PIPELINE

    def analyze(self, text: str) -> Dict[str, object]:
        """
        Analyze a single text string and return a dict:
        {
            'model': 'vader' or 'transformer',
            'label': 'positive'|'negative'|'neutral' (or 'positive'/'negative' for SST-2),
            'score': float in [-1.0, 1.0] for Vader, or [0.0, 1.0] for transformer,
            'details': original score dict (optional)
        }
        """
        if self.method == "vader":
            scores = self.analyzer.polarity_scores(text)
            compound = float(scores.get("compound", 0.0))
            if compound >= 0.05:
                label = "positive"
            elif compound <= -0.05:
                label = "negative"
            else:
                label = "neutral"
            return {
                "model": "vader",
                "label": label,
                "score": compound,
                "details": scores,
            }
        else:
            # Transformer path
            results = self.pipeline(text)
            if isinstance(results, list) and len(results) > 0:
                r = results[0]
                label = str(r.get("label", "neutral")).lower()
                score = float(r.get("score", 0.0))
                return {
                    "model": "transformer",
                    "label": label,
                    "score": score,
                    "details": r,
                }
            else:
                return {
                    "model": "transformer",
                    "label": "neutral",
                    "score": 0.0,
                    "details": {},
                }

def clean_text(text: str) -> str:
    """
    Lightweight preprocessing for social media text.
    - Replace URLs with a placeholder
    - Remove mentions
    - Collapse whitespace
    - Optional: remove trailing hashtags or keep them (here we keep them)
    """
    text = re.sub(r"http\S+", "URL", text)      # URLs
    text = re.sub(r"www\.\S+", "URL", text)     # URLs
    text = re.sub(r"@\w+", "", text)            # mentions
    text = re.sub(r"\s+#", " #", text)          # ensure spacing before hashtags
    text = re.sub(r"\s+", " ", text)            # collapse whitespace
    return text.strip()

def analyze_posts(posts: List[str], analyzer: SentimentAnalyzer) -> pd.DataFrame:
    """
    Analyze a list of post texts and return a DataFrame with results.
    Columns: id, text, clean_text, model, label, score
    """
    rows = []
    for i, text in enumerate(posts):
        clean = clean_text(text)
        result = analyzer.analyze(clean)
        rows.append({
            "id": i,
            "text": text,
            "clean_text": clean,
            "model": result["model"],
            "label": result["label"],
            "score": result["score"],
        })
    return pd.DataFrame(rows)

def load_posts_from_csv(path: str, text_col: str = "text") -> pd.DataFrame:
    """
    Load posts from a CSV file. Expects a column with text data.
    Returns a DataFrame with at least the text column.
    """
    df = pd.read_csv(path)
    if text_col not in df.columns:
        raise ValueError(f"Column '{text_col}' not found in CSV.")
    return df

def save_results(df: pd.DataFrame, path: str) -> None:
    df.to_csv(path, index=False)

if __name__ == "__main__":
    # Example usage
    sample_posts = [
        "I love this product! 😍 The new update is amazing. #awesome",
        "Ugh, the app keeps crashing... so frustrating. @support http://example.com",
        "Meh, it's okay I guess. Nothing special but not bad either.",
        "Can't believe how slow the service was today. Worst day ever.",
        "Just tried the new feature and it's fantastic! 10/10"
    ]

    # Initialize analyzer (default: VADER)
    analyzer = SentimentAnalyzer(method="vader")

    # Analyze in-memory posts
    df_results = analyze_posts(sample_posts, analyzer)
    print(df_results)

    # If you have a CSV with a column 'text', you can do:
    # df = load_posts_from_csv("social_posts.csv", text_col="text")
    # df_results = analyze_posts(df["text"].tolist(), analyzer)

    # analyzer_tf = SentimentAnalyzer(method="transformer")
    # df_results_tf = analyze_posts(sample_posts, analyzer_tf)
    # print(df_results_tf)

I’ll start with the necessary imports, set the hyperparameters, and load the IMDb dataset, keeping in mind that this dataset contains 25,000 training and 25,000 test reviews when using the top 10,000 words. 

After padding the sequences, I’ll build the model, compile it, and train it, including optional steps for saving and predicting on samples. I should also mention variations like using a Bidirectional LSTM for better performance, ensuring it's all clear and runs with TensorFlow 2.x!</think> Here's a self-contained Python script that trains a sentiment classifier using an LSTM with the IMDb dataset (in TensorFlow 2.x / tf.keras). It uses a basic Embedding + LSTM architecture and should run out of the box.

Code (copy-paste into a .py file or a notebook cell):

```python
import numpy as np
import tensorflow as tf
from tensorflow.keras.datasets import imdb
from tensorflow.keras.preprocessing.sequence import pad_sequences
from tensorflow.keras.models import Sequential
from tensorflow.keras.layers import Embedding, LSTM, Dense, Dropout

# Hyperparameters
VOCAB_SIZE = 10000      # use the top 10k words
MAX_LEN = 500           # max sequence length (in words)
EMBEDDING_DIM = 128
LSTM_UNITS = 64
BATCH_SIZE = 64
EPOCHS = 3

# 1) Load data (IMDb: 0 = negative, 1 = positive)
print("Loading data...")
(x_train, y_train), (x_test, y_test) = imdb.load_data(num_words=VOCAB_SIZE)

# 2) Preprocess: pad sequences to the same length
print("Padding sequences...")
x_train_padded = pad_sequences(x_train, maxlen=MAX_LEN, padding='post', truncating='post')
x_test_padded  = pad_sequences(x_test,  maxlen=MAX_LEN, padding='post', truncating='post')

# 3) Build model
print("Building model...")
model = Sequential([
    Embedding(input_dim=VOCAB_SIZE, output_dim=EMBEDDING_DIM, input_length=MAX_LEN),
    LSTM(LSTM_UNITS, dropout=0.2, recurrent_dropout=0.2),
    Dense(1, activation='sigmoid')
])

model.compile(optimizer='adam',
              loss='binary_crossentropy',
              metrics=['accuracy'])

model.summary()

# 4) Train
print("Training...")
history = model.fit(
    x_train_padded, y_train,
    validation_split=0.2,
    epochs=EPOCHS,
    batch_size=BATCH_SIZE,
    verbose=2
)

# 5) Evaluate
print("Evaluating on test data...")
loss, acc = model.evaluate(x_test_padded, y_test, batch_size=BATCH_SIZE)
print(f"Test loss: {loss:.4f}, Test accuracy: {acc:.4f}")

# 6) Save the model (optional)
model.save("sentiment_lstm_imdb.h5")

# Optional: quick inference on a sample (uses pre-padded test data for demonstration)
sample_idx = 0
sample_seq = x_test_padded[sample_idx:sample_idx+1]
pred = model.predict(sample_seq)
print(f"Sample prediction (0=neg, 1=pos): {float(pred[0][0]):.4f}  (true label: {y_test[sample_idx]})")
```

Notes and optional extensions

- If you want to try a more expressive model, you can use a Bidirectional LSTM:
  - from tensorflow.keras.layers import Bidirectional
  - Replace the LSTM layer with: Bidirectional(LSTM(LSTM_UNITS, dropout=0.2, recurrent_dropout=0.2))
- For improved performance on domain-specific data, consider:
  - Increasing MAX_LEN and/or VOCAB_SIZE
  - Using a pre-trained embedding (e.g., GloVe) and an Embedding layer initialized with those weights
  - Stacking multiple LSTM layers or using GRU cells
- If you have your own labeled text data, you can adapt the script to use a Tokenizer and text_to_sequences instead of the IMDb dataset:
  - Build a Tokenizer on your texts
  - Convert texts to sequences with tokenizer.texts_to_sequences(...)
  - Pad sequences with pad_sequences
  - Train the same model structure (embedding + LSTM + dense)

This script should get you started with a solid baseline for text sentiment classification using an LSTM. If you want, I can tailor a version for a custom dataset or show how to add a Bidirectional LSTM.

The rule that any number multiplied by zero results in zero stems from how multiplication is defined and its algebraic properties. Zero acts as an absorbing element in multiplication. 

- Intuition: zero signifies "no quantity"; multiplying by zero means having no copies of anything, resulting in nothing.
- For natural numbers: a * 0 is the sum of zero terms, which equals zero.

This explanation captures the essence of zero in multiplication!</think> Here’s why the rule holds, in both intuitive and formal terms.

- Intuition: Zero means “none.” If you have zero copies of something, you have nothing at all. Multiplying any number by zero is like counting that quantity zero times, so you get zero.

- Natural-number view (repeated addition): For natural numbers, multiplication a × n means adding a to itself n times. If n = 0, you add a zero times, i.e., you form the sum of zero terms, which by convention is 0. So a × 0 = 0 (and similarly 0 × a = 0 when you view 0 as adding zero a times).

- Formal justification (distributive law): In arithmetic with real numbers (or any ring), multiplication distributes over addition: a × (b + c) = a × b + a × c. Take b = 0 and c = 0:
  a × (0 + 0) = a × 0 + a × 0.
  Since 0 + 0 = 0, the left side is a × 0, so a × 0 = a × 0 + a × 0.
  Subtract a × 0 from both sides (using additive inverses) to get 0 = a × 0. Hence a × 0 = 0 for any a.
  By commutativity of multiplication, 0 × a = a × 0 = 0 as well.

- Takeaway: Zero acts as an absorbing element for multiplication: multiplying any number by zero yields zero. This is consistent with the idea of zero as “nothing” and with the basic laws (distributivity, additive identity) that define arithmetic.

I think sticking to about 300-700 words will keep everything concise yet thorough.</think> Prime numbers are central to modern cryptography because they enable certain mathematical problems to be easy to perform in one direction but hard to reverse without special information. Here’s how that idea plays out in practice:

- Core hardness: Many cryptosystems rely on problems that are easy to compute in the forward direction but believed hard to reverse. For RSA, the public modulus n is the product of two large primes p and q. Multiplying p and q is easy, but factoring n back into p and q (and thus breaking the system) is believed to be very hard for suitably large primes. The security rests on the difficulty of factorization of semiprimes (numbers with exactly two prime factors).

- RSA in detail (primes enable key structure): In RSA, choose large primes p and q, form n = p·q, and pick an exponent e that is coprime to φ(n) = (p−1)(q−1). The private key d is the modular inverse of e modulo φ(n). Without knowing p and q (and thus φ(n)), deriving d is effectively as hard as factoring n. The primes are what give you a modulus with a structure that attackers can’t easily reverse.

- Discrete logarithm and Diffie–Hellman: In protocols like Diffie–Hellman, you work in a finite group (commonly the multiplicative group modulo a large prime p, or a group defined by an elliptic curve). The security relies on the hardness of the discrete logarithm problem modulo p (or on the elliptic-curve discrete log problem). Choosing a large prime p (and often a “safe” prime where (p−1)/2 is prime) makes the discrete log problem computationally intractable for attackers.

- Elliptic curve cryptography (ECC): ECC uses algebraic structures defined over prime fields (or binary fields). The security of ECC rests on the elliptic curve discrete logarithm problem (ECDLP). Because the underlying group is defined over a prime field, you can achieve comparable security with much smaller key sizes than RSA, thanks to the properties of primes in that setting.

- Prime generation and primes’ properties: In practice, primes must be large and chosen carefully. Primality testing (deterministic for certain sizes, or probabilistic like Miller–Rabin) is used to generate candidate primes quickly. Prime sizes (e.g., 2048-bit primes for RSA today) are driven by the need to resist factoring and discrete-log attacks with current algorithms. Some primes are also chosen with special properties (e.g., safe primes p where (p−1)/2 is prime) to defend against specific attack vectors like certain subgroup attacks in DH.

- Why not composite moduli or non-prime bases?: If you used integers that aren’t built from primes in these constructions, the underlying hard problems either don’t exist or become much easier to solve. Primes endow the arithmetic with strong, well-studied hardness assumptions that are the backbone of security proofs and practical schemes.

- Practical considerations and evolving threats: The effectiveness of prime-based schemes depends on the continued difficulty of factoring or discrete-log problems. Advances in algorithms or hardware (or quantum computing, via Shor’s algorithm) could undermine current choices, which is why key sizes scale up and post-quantum cryptography research often looks beyond traditional prime-based assumptions.

In short, primes are pivotal because they enable the hard math behind the most widely used public-key cryptosystems. They provide the structure (via factoring hardness, discrete-log hardness, and well-behaved arithmetic in finite fields) that makes it feasible to use public keys securely while keeping private keys recoverable only to those who possess the secret information.

It uses generators to yield steps (array snapshot and highlighted indices) so the bars animate as the sort progresses.

- Press:

  - q for Quick Sort

```python
import random
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from matplotlib.animation import FuncAnimation

# Sorting algorithm generators

def bubble_sort_gen(arr):
    n = len(arr)
    for i in range(n):
        for j in range(0, n - i - 1):
            if arr[j] > arr[j + 1]:
                arr[j], arr[j + 1] = arr[j + 1], arr[j]
                yield (arr.copy(), ('swap', j, j + 1))
    # final state (no specific swap info)
    yield (arr.copy(), ('range', 0, n - 1))

def partition(arr, low, high):
    pivot = arr[high]
    i = low
    for j in range(low, high):
        if arr[j] <= pivot:
            arr[i], arr[j] = arr[j], arr[i]
            yield (arr.copy(), ('swap', i, j))
            i += 1
    arr[i], arr[high] = arr[high], arr[i]
    yield (arr.copy(), ('swap', i, high))
    return i

def quick_sort_gen(arr, low, high):
    if low < high:
        p = yield from partition(arr, low, high)
        yield from quick_sort_gen(arr, low, p - 1)
        yield from quick_sort_gen(arr, p + 1, high)

# Quick sort entry
def quick_sort_steps(arr):
    yield from quick_sort_gen(arr, 0, len(arr) - 1)

def merge_sort_gen(arr, l, r):
    if l < r:
        mid = (l + r) // 2
        yield from merge_sort_gen(arr, l, mid)
        yield from merge_sort_gen(arr, mid + 1, r)
        yield from merge_merge(arr, l, mid, r)

def merge_merge(arr, l, mid, r):
    left = arr[l:mid + 1]
    right = arr[mid + 1:r + 1]
    i = j = 0
    k = l
    while i < len(left) and j < len(right):
        if left[i] <= right[j]:
            arr[k] = left[i]
            i += 1
        else:
            arr[k] = right[j]
            j += 1
        k += 1
        yield (arr.copy(), ('range', l, r))
    while i < len(left):
        arr[k] = left[i]
        i += 1
        k += 1
        yield (arr.copy(), ('range', l, r))
    while j < len(right):
        arr[k] = right[j]
        j += 1
        k += 1
        yield (arr.copy(), ('range', l, r))

# Merge sort entry
def merge_sort_steps(arr):
    yield from merge_sort_gen(arr, 0, len(arr) - 1)

# Visualization class
class SortingVisualizer:
    def __init__(self, n=60, interval=40, seed=None):
        self.n = n
        self.interval = interval  # ms between frames
        if seed is not None:
            random.seed(seed)

        # Original and current array
        self.original = [random.randint(1, 100) for _ in range(n)]
        self.arr = self.original.copy()

        # Matplotlib setup
        self.fig, self.ax = plt.subplots()
        self.ax.set_title("Sorting Visualizer - Press b/q/m to choose algorithm; r to randomize; Space to pause")
        self.ax.set_xlim(0, n)
        self.ax.set_ylim(0, max(self.arr) * 1.15 if self.arr else 1)

        self.bars = self.ax.bar(range(n), self.arr, align='edge', color='steelblue', width=0.8)
        self.ax.set_xlabel("Index")
        self.ax.set_ylabel("Value")

        # Interaction/state
        self.gen = None
        self.running = True
        self.current_algo = None

        # Animation
        self.anim = FuncAnimation(self.fig, self._update, init_func=self._init_plot,
                                  interval=self.interval, blit=True)

        # Keyboard controls
        self.fig.canvas.mpl_connect('key_press_event', self._on_key)

    def _init_plot(self):
        # Initial drawing of bars
        for bar, val in zip(self.bars, self.arr):
            bar.set_height(val)
            bar.set_color('steelblue')
        self.ax.set_ylim(0, max(self.arr) * 1.15 if self.arr else 1)
        return self.bars

    def _on_key(self, event):
        key = event.key
        if key in ('b', 'B'):
            self.start_bubble()
        elif key in ('q', 'Q'):
            self.start_quick()
        elif key in ('m', 'M'):
            self.start_merge()
        elif key in ('r', 'R'):
            self.randomize()
        elif key == ' ':
            self.running = not self.running

    def randomize(self):
        self.original = [random.randint(1, 100) for _ in range(self.n)]
        self.arr = self.original.copy()
        for bar, v in zip(self.bars, self.arr):
            bar.set_height(v)
            bar.set_color('steelblue')
        self.ax.set_ylim(0, max(self.arr) * 1.15 if self.arr else 1)
        self.gen = None
        self.current_algo = None
        self.ax.set_title("Sorting Visualizer - Fresh array")
        self.fig.canvas.draw_idle()

    def start_bubble(self):
        self.arr = self.original.copy()
        for bar, v in zip(self.bars, self.arr):
            bar.set_height(v)
            bar.set_color('steelblue')
        self.gen = bubble_sort_gen(self.arr)
        self.current_algo = 'Bubble Sort'
        self.ax.set_title("Bubble Sort")
        self.fig.canvas.draw_idle()

    def start_quick(self):
        self.arr = self.original.copy()
        for bar, v in zip(self.bars, self.arr):
            bar.set_height(v)
            bar.set_color('steelblue')
        self.gen = quick_sort_steps(self.arr)
        self.current_algo = 'Quick Sort'
        self.ax.set_title("Quick Sort")
        self.fig.canvas.draw_idle()

    def start_merge(self):
        self.arr = self.original.copy()
        for bar, v in zip(self.bars, self.arr):
            bar.set_height(v)
            bar.set_color('steelblue')
        self.gen = merge_sort_steps(self.arr)
        self.current_algo = 'Merge Sort'
        self.ax.set_title("Merge Sort")
        self.fig.canvas.draw_idle()

    def _update(self, frame):
        if not self.running or self.gen is None:
            return self.bars

        try:
            step = next(self.gen)
        except StopIteration:
            self.gen = None
            self.ax.set_title("Sorting completed.")
            return self.bars

        # step is a tuple: (array_snapshot, info)
        if not isinstance(step, tuple) or len(step) != 2:
            return self.bars

        arr_snapshot, info = step
        # Update heights
        for bar, val in zip(self.bars, arr_snapshot):
            bar.set_height(val)

        # Visual highlights based on info
        # info formats:
        # - ('swap', i, j)
        # - ('range', l, r)
        if isinstance(info, tuple) and len(info) >= 1:
            tag = info[0]

            if tag == 'swap' and len(info) == 3:
                i, j = info[1], info[2]
                for idx, bar in enumerate(self.bars):
                    if idx == i or idx == j:
                        bar.set_color('orange')
                    else:
                        bar.set_color('steelblue')
            elif tag == 'range' and len(info) == 3:
                l, r = info[1], info[2]
                for idx, bar in enumerate(self.bars):
                    if l <= idx <= r:
                        bar.set_color('lightgreen')
                    else:
                        bar.set_color('steelblue')
            else:
                # Unknown info, reset colors
                for bar in self.bars:
                    bar.set_color('steelblue')
        else:
            for bar in self.bars:
                bar.set_color('steelblue')

        return self.bars

    def run(self):
        plt.show()


if __name__ == '__main__':
    vis = SortingVisualizer(n=60, interval=40, seed=42)
    print("Controls:")
    print("  b - Bubble Sort")
    print("  q - Quick Sort")
    print("  m - Merge Sort")
    print("  r - Randomize new array")
    print("  Space - Pause/Resume")
    vis.run()
```

I’ll present the code as a plain text block, ensuring it’s a single Python script that the user can run. This script will be named `predator_prey_lv.py` and will include necessary imports, a `lotka_volterra` function, and a `main()` function to set parameters and run the solver.

Let’s finalize this!</think> Here is a self-contained Python script that implements a basic Lotka-Volterra predator-prey model. It uses SciPy's solver if available, and falls back to a simple Euler method otherwise.

- Prey: x
- Predator: y
- dx/dt = alpha*x - beta*x*y
- dy/dt = delta*x*y - gamma*y

Parameters (typical values): alpha=0.6, beta=0.02, delta=0.8, gamma=0.6
Initial conditions: x0=40, y0=9

Code:

```python
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

# Lotka-Volterra right-hand side
def lotka_volterra_rhs(t, z, alpha, beta, delta, gamma):
    x, y = z
    dxdt = alpha*x - beta*x*y
    dydt = delta*x*y - gamma*y
    return [dxdt, dydt]

def simulate_with_scipy(alpha, beta, delta, gamma, x0, y0, t_span, t_eval):
    try:
        from scipy.integrate import solve_ivp
    except Exception:
        return None  # SciPy not available

    sol = solve_ivp(
        fun=lambda t, z: lotka_volterra_rhs(t, z, alpha, beta, delta, gamma),
        t_span=t_span,
        y0=[x0, y0],
        t_eval=t_eval,
        method='RK45',
        vectorized=False
    )
    if not sol.success:
        raise RuntimeError("ODE solver failed.")
    return sol.t, sol.y

def simulate_with_euler(alpha, beta, delta, gamma, x0, y0, t_span, dt):
    t0, t_end = t_span
    t_values = np.arange(t0, t_end + dt, dt)
    x = np.zeros(len(t_values))
    y = np.zeros(len(t_values))
    x[0] = x0
    y[0] = y0
    for i in range(len(t_values) - 1):
        dx = alpha*x[i] - beta*x[i]*y[i]
        dy = delta*x[i]*y[i] - gamma*y[i]
        x_next = x[i] + dt*dx
        y_next = y[i] + dt*dy
        x[i+1] = max(0.0, x_next)
        y[i+1] = max(0.0, y_next)
    return t_values, np.array([x, y])

def main():
    # Parameters
    alpha = 0.6   # prey growth rate
    beta = 0.02   # predation rate
    delta = 0.8   # predator reproduction per prey eaten
    gamma = 0.6    # predator mortality

    # Initial conditions
    x0 = 40.0  # initial prey
    y0 = 9.0   # initial predators

    # Time grid
    t_span = (0.0, 200.0)
    t_eval = np.linspace(t_span[0], t_span[1], 1000)
    dt = 0.01  # for Euler if SciPy is not available

    # Try SciPy solver first
    result = simulate_with_scipy(alpha, beta, delta, gamma, x0, y0, t_span, t_eval)
    if result is not None:
        t, Z = result
        prey, pred = Z
    else:
        # Fallback to Euler method
        t, Z = simulate_with_euler(alpha, beta, delta, gamma, x0, y0, t_span, dt)
        prey, pred = Z

    # Plot results
    plt.figure(figsize=(8, 5))
    plt.plot(t, prey, label='Prey')
    plt.plot(t, pred, label='Predator')
    plt.xlabel('Time')
    plt.ylabel('Population')
    plt.title('Lotka-Volterra Predator-Prey Model')
    plt.legend()
    plt.grid(True)
    plt.tight_layout()
    plt.show()

    # Optional: print final populations
    print(f"Final prey: {prey[-1]:.2f}, Final predators: {pred[-1]:.2f}")

if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()
```

Notes:
- If SciPy is installed, the script uses a robust RK45 solver with adaptive stepping.
- If SciPy is not available, it falls back to a simple explicit Euler integration (note that Euler can be less stable for stiff or long simulations; you can increase accuracy by reducing dt).
- You can tweak the parameters and initial conditions to explore different dynamics (cycles, damped/unstable oscillations).

  <script>
    (function() {
      const openBtn = document.getElementById('openNewsletter');
      const overlay = document.getElementById('overlay');
      const modal = document.getElementById('newsletterModal');
      const closeBtn = document.getElementById('closeModal');
      const form = document.getElementById('newsletterForm');
      const status = document.getElementById('formStatus');
      const formArea = document.getElementById('newsletterForm'); // entire form is the area to show/hide fields

      // Simple focus trap within modal
      let focusableElements;
      let firstFocusable;
      let lastFocusable;

      function openModal() {
        // Show overlay and modal with animation
        overlay.classList.add('show');
        modal.classList.add('show');
        overlay.setAttribute('aria-hidden', 'false');
        modal.setAttribute('aria-hidden', 'false');
        // Prevent background scroll
        document.body.style.overflow = 'hidden';

        // Prepare focus trap
        focusableElements = modal.querySelectorAll('a[href], button:not([disabled]), input:not([disabled]), select:not([disabled]), textarea:not([disabled])');
        firstFocusable = focusableElements[0];
        lastFocusable = focusableElements[focusableElements.length - 1];

        // Focus the first input in the modal (if present) otherwise the modal itself
        const firstInput = modal.querySelector('input, button, select, textarea');
        (firstInput || modal).focus();

        document.addEventListener('keydown', trapTabKey);
      }

      function closeModal() {
        overlay.classList.remove('show');
        modal.classList.remove('show');
        overlay.setAttribute('aria-hidden', 'true');
        modal.setAttribute('aria-hidden', 'true');
        document.body.style.overflow = '';

        // Remove focus trap
        document.removeEventListener('keydown', trapTabKey);

        // Reset form and status for next open
        status.style.display = 'none';
        status.textContent = '';
        // Ensure form is visible again if it was hidden after success
        // (Reset any prior success view)
        // Re-enable form fields
        let formChildren = form.querySelectorAll('.field, .actions');
        formChildren.forEach(el => el.style.display = '');
        // Reset form values
        form.reset();
        // Return focus to the trigger button for accessibility
        openBtn.focus();
      }

      function trapTabKey(e) {
        if (e.key === 'Escape') {
          e.preventDefault();
          closeModal();
          return;
        }
        if (e.key !== 'Tab') return;

        // Shift+Tab -> move to last, Tab -> move to first
        const active = document.activeElement;
        if (e.shiftKey) {
          if (active === firstFocusable) {
            e.preventDefault();
            lastFocusable.focus();
          }
        } else {
          if (active === lastFocusable) {
            e.preventDefault();
            firstFocusable.focus();
          }
        }
      }

      // Open/close event bindings
      openBtn.addEventListener('click', openModal);
      closeBtn.addEventListener('click', closeModal);
      overlay.addEventListener('click', closeModal);

      // Also close when pressing Enter on overlay? Not required; overlay click is enough.

      // Form submission
      form.addEventListener('submit', function(e) {
        e.preventDefault();
        const emailInput = document.getElementById('email');
        const nameInput = document.getElementById('name');
        const frequencyInput = document.getElementById('frequency');
        const email = emailInput.value.trim();
        const name = nameInput.value.trim();
        const freq = frequencyInput.value;

        // Very basic validation
        const isValid = email.length > 0 && email.includes('@') && email.includes('.');
        if (!isValid) {
          status.className = 'status error';
          status.textContent = 'Please enter a valid email address to continue.';
          status.style.display = 'block';
          emailInput.focus();
          return;
        }

        // Success view
        status.className = 'status';
        status.style.display = 'block';
        status.textContent = `Thanks${name ? ' ' + name : ''}! You have subscribed to the ${freq} newsletter.`;
        // Hide the form fields and show only the status message
        // We simply hide the form controls to show the status
        const fields = form.querySelectorAll('.field, .actions');
        fields.forEach(el => el.style.display = 'none');
      });

      // Optional: close modal on Escape from anywhere (already handled in trapTabKey)
      // Initialize: keep modal hidden on load
    })();
  </script>
</body>
</html>
```

Notes
- The modal opens with a fade/scale animation and traps focus inside it for accessibility.
- Clicking outside the modal (overlay) or pressing Esc closes the modal.
- The form validates the email (basic check) and, on success, shows a friendly message while hiding the form fields.
- The styling uses CSS transitions for a smooth feel and respects users who prefer reduced motion. If needed, you can tweak colors, sizes, or animation timing.

General steps
- Yes, the divisor must be nonzero (cannot be 0).
- Write the dividend (the three-digit number) under the long-division symbol and the one-digit divisor to the outside left.
- Look at the leftmost part of the dividend that is at least as big as the divisor. If the first digit is smaller than the divisor, take the first two digits (and sometimes the first three, but with a 3-digit dividend and 1-digit divisor you’ll usually use the first two digits).
- Determine how many times the divisor fits into that part. This is the next digit of the quotient.
- Multiply the divisor by that quotient digit, write the product under the part you used, and subtract to get a remainder.
- Bring down the next digit of the dividend to form a new number.
- Repeat the process until you’ve used all digits of the dividend.
- If you want decimals, after finishing the whole number part, place the decimal point in the quotient and continue by bringing down zeros (this gives as many decimal places as you need).

Example 1: 357 ÷ 4
- 4 doesn’t fit into 3, so consider 35.
- 4 goes into 35 eight times (8 × 4 = 32). Write 8 on the quotient line.
- Subtract: 35 − 32 = 3.
- Bring down the next digit (7) to make 37.
- 4 goes into 37 nine times (9 × 4 = 36). Write 9 next to the 8.
- Subtract: 37 − 36 = 1. No more digits to bring down, so this is the remainder.
- So far: 357 ÷ 4 = 89 with remainder 1.
- If you want a decimal, continue: bring down a 0 to get 10. 4 goes into 10 two times (2 × 4 = 8). Remainder 2.
- Bring down another 0 to get 20. 4 goes into 20 five times (5 × 4 = 20). Remainder 0.
- Decimal form: 357 ÷ 4 = 89.25.

Example 2: 804 ÷ 3
- 3 goes into 8 two times (2 × 3 = 6). Write 2 on the quotient.
- Subtract: 8 − 6 = 2. Bring down the next digit (0) to get 20.
- 3 goes into 20 six times (6 × 3 = 18). Subtract: 20 − 18 = 2.
- Bring down the next digit (4) to get 24.

- No remainder. Quotient is 268.
- Decimal not needed here since remainder is 0.

Tips
- A good quick check: quotient × divisor + remainder should equal the original dividend.
- If the leftmost digit of the dividend is smaller than the divisor, you must take more digits (as shown in the first step of the examples).

Let's make sure it’s all straightforward and easy to follow!</think> Here is a self-contained Python script to perform sentiment analysis on tweets using an LSTM model with TensorFlow/Keras. The script expects a CSV file with at least two columns: tweet text and label (0 = negative, 1 = positive). Adjust column names if your file differs.

What it does:
- Cleans tweet text (lowercasing, removing URLs, mentions, hashtags, non-letters)
- Tokenizes text and creates padded sequences
- Builds a Bidirectional LSTM model with an Embedding layer
- Trains with early stopping
- Evaluates on a held-out test set
- Provides a simple predict function for new tweets
- Saves the model and tokenizer

Code (save as train_lstm_sentiment_tweets.py or run in a notebook):

```python
import re
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split
from sklearn.metrics import classification_report, accuracy_score
import tensorflow as tf
from tensorflow.keras.preprocessing.text import Tokenizer
from tensorflow.keras.preprocessing.sequence import pad_sequences
from tensorflow.keras.models import Sequential
from tensorflow.keras.layers import Embedding, LSTM, Bidirectional, Dropout, Dense
from tensorflow.keras.callbacks import EarlyStopping
import json

# ------------------------
# Text cleaning function
# ------------------------
def clean_text(text: str) -> str:
    text = text.lower()
    # Remove URLs
    text = re.sub(r'http\S+|www\S+|https\S+', '', text)
    # Remove user mentions
    text = re.sub(r'@\w+', '', text)
    # Remove hashtags (keep the word if you want to remove #)
    text = re.sub(r'#\w+', '', text)
    # Remove non-letters
    text = re.sub(r'[^a-z\s]', ' ', text)
    # Normalize whitespace
    text = re.sub(r'\s+', ' ', text).strip()
    return text

# ------------------------
# Load data
# ------------------------
# Path to your dataset. Expect columns: 'tweet' (or 'text') and 'label' (0/1)
DATA_PATH = 'data/tweets.csv'  # adjust as needed

df = pd.read_csv(DATA_PATH)

# Adjust column names if your CSV uses different ones
text_col = 'tweet'   # e.g., 'tweet' or 'text'
label_col = 'label'    # e.g., 'label'

df = df[[text_col, label_col]].dropna()
df[text_col] = df[text_col].astype(str).apply(clean_text)

texts = df[text_col].tolist()
labels = df[label_col].tolist()

# ------------------------
# Train/Validation split
# ------------------------
X_train, X_val, y_train, y_val = train_test_split(
    texts, labels, test_size=0.2, random_state=42, stratify=labels
)

# ------------------------
# Tokenization / Sequencing
# ------------------------
MAX_FEATURES = 20000  # vocabulary size
MAX_LEN = 50          # max sequence length (pads/truncates to this length)
EMBEDDING_DIM = 100

tokenizer = Tokenizer(num_words=MAX_FEATURES, oov_token='<OOV>')
tokenizer.fit_on_texts(X_train)

def texts_to_padded(sequences_texts):
    seq = tokenizer.texts_to_sequences(sequences_texts)
    padded = pad_sequences(seq, maxlen=MAX_LEN, padding='post', truncating='post')
    return padded

X_train_seq = texts_to_padded(X_train)
X_val_seq = texts_to_padded(X_val)

# ------------------------
# Build the model
# ------------------------
vocab_size = MAX_FEATURES + 1  # +1 because index 0 is padding

model = Sequential([
    Embedding(input_dim=vocab_size, output_dim=EMBEDDING_DIM, input_length=MAX_LEN),
    Bidirectional(LSTM(64, return_sequences=False)),
    Dropout(0.5),
    Dense(1, activation='sigmoid')
])

model.compile(loss='binary_crossentropy', optimizer='adam', metrics=['accuracy'])

model.summary()

# ------------------------
# Train
# ------------------------
early_stop = EarlyStopping(monitor='val_loss', patience=3, restore_best_weights=True)

history = model.fit(
    X_train_seq, np.array(y_train),
    validation_data=(X_val_seq, np.array(y_val)),
    batch_size=128,
    epochs=10,
    callbacks=[early_stop],
    verbose=1
)

# ------------------------
# Evaluate
# ------------------------
y_val_pred_prob = model.predict(X_val_seq)
y_val_pred = (y_val_pred_prob > 0.5).astype(int).flatten()

print("Validation Accuracy:", accuracy_score(y_val, y_val_pred))
print("\nClassification Report:")
print(classification_report(y_val, y_val_pred, digits=4))

# ------------------------
# Save model & tokenizer
# ------------------------
MODEL_PATH = 'tweet_lstm_sentiment.h5'
MODEL_JSON = 'tokenizer.json'

model.save(MODEL_PATH)
# Save tokenizer for future use
with open(MODEL_JSON, 'w', encoding='utf-8') as f:
    json.dump(tokenizer.to_json(), f, ensure_ascii=False)

# ------------------------
# Predict function for new tweets
# ------------------------
def predict_sentiment(text: str):
    cleaned = clean_text(text)
    seq = tokenizer.texts_to_sequences([cleaned])
    padded = pad_sequences(seq, maxlen=MAX_LEN, padding='post')
    prob = model.predict(padded)[0][0]
    label = int(prob >= 0.5)
    sentiment = 'positive' if label == 1 else 'negative'
    return sentiment, float(prob)

# Example usage:
# sentiment, prob = predict_sentiment("I love this product! It's amazing.")
# print(sentiment, prob)
```

Notes and tips:
- Data: Replace the DATA_PATH and column names if your dataset uses different headers (e.g., csv with columns "text" and "sentiment"). Ensure labels are 0/1.
- Cleaning: The clean_text function can be adjusted to keep or remove hashtags, emojis, or numbers, depending on your needs.
- Hyperparameters: You may want to tune MAX_FEATURES, MAX_LEN, and LSTM units for your dataset size. For very large datasets, consider reducing MAX_LEN or using a smaller model to fit resources.
- Embeddings: If you have pre-trained embeddings (e.g., GloVe Twitter vectors), you can load them into the Embedding layer to potentially improve results. This script uses a trainable embedding from scratch.
- Saving/loading: The script saves the model and the tokenizer. For loading later, reconstruct the tokenizer from the saved json and load the model with tf.keras.models.load_model.

What “objective morality” would mean
- Objective morality = there are moral facts or truths that do not depend on what anyone believes or what culture says.
- Anti-objectivity (relativism/subjectivism) = moral verdicts depend on cultural norms or individual attitudes; there aren’t mind-independent moral facts.

Main positions

1) Moral realism / moral objectivity
- There are mind-independent moral facts (e.g., harming innocents is wrong).
- Variants:
  - Naturalistic realism: moral facts are natural properties (adjacent to science in some theories).
  - Non-naturalist realism: moral properties are not natural properties (G.E. Moore’s tradition, etc.).
  - Constructive or rationalist realism (Korsgaard, Rawls): moral requirements arise from rational constraints or fair principles.
- Pros often cited:
  - Explains moral disagreement as a clash with reality rather than mere opinion.
  - Supports the idea of moral progress (societies can get morally closer to the truth).
  - Provides a strong basis for universal duties or rights.
- Common challenges:
  - What exactly are these facts? How do we know them? Is there a legitimate “moral science”?
  - The is-ought problem: deriving oughts from is-statements is philosophically tricky.

2) Anti-realism: cultural or moral relativism; subjectivism; expressivism
- Cultural relativism: morality is determined by cultural norms; there are no universal moral facts.
- Moral subjectivism: moral judgments express personal attitudes rather than facts.
- Expressivism / Emotivism: moral statements express emotional stance or prescriptions, not facts.
- Pros often cited:
  - Explains deep cross-cultural disagreements and variations without forcing a single truth behind all cultures.
  - Avoids the problem of identifying objective moral facts in areas where cultures clearly differ.
- Common challenges:
  - If morality is just culture-relative, how can we criticize seriously immoral practices in other cultures?
  - How do we account for apparent moral progress or moral reform if there are no objective standards?
  - The claim that “it’s wrong to torture” sounds like a fact claim, not only an attitude.

3) Constructivism and “rational” objectivity
- Morality arises from rational agreement among agents (e.g., Rawls, Korsgaard). There are objective requirements that flow from rational procedures or from the coherence of a just system.
- Pros:
  - Provides a middle ground: reasons and rights are objective in a rational sense, even if they are grounded in human perspectives.
  - Allows for universal norms without claiming they exist as mind-independent facts in the world.
- Challenges:
  - Why should rational agreement be the ultimate authority? Different ways of reasoning can produce different conclusions.

4) Other important lines
- Divine command theory: morality depends on God’s commands. Some see this as objective (grounded in God), others see it as recasting objective norms as God’s will.
- Moral realism with evolutionary considerations: some think our moral beliefs track adaptive truth conditions, which can look objective but may be shaped by biology and culture.

What this means in practice
- If you think morality is objective, you’ll seek universal, rationally defensible principles (rights, duties, harm, fairness) that apply to all.
- If you think morality is relative or subjective, you’ll emphasize cultural sensitivity, tolerance for difference, and local norms—often with caution about condemning other cultures.
- Many people adopt a middle-ground stance: there are objective elements (certain basic principles or rational requirements) but plenty of variation in how those principles are interpreted or implemented across cultures.

    </div>
  </div>

  <script>
    (function () {
      const openBtn = document.getElementById('openModal');
      const overlay = document.getElementById('overlay');
      const modal = document.getElementById('modal');
      const closeBtn = document.getElementById('closeModal');
      const header = document.getElementById('modalHeader');

      // Open / close logic
      function openModal() {
        overlay.classList.add('active');
        overlay.setAttribute('aria-hidden', 'false');
        document.body.classList.add('no-scroll');
        // Optional: focus the modal for accessibility
        modal.setAttribute('tabindex', '-1');
        modal.focus?.();
      }

      function closeModal() {
        overlay.classList.remove('active');
        overlay.setAttribute('aria-hidden', 'true');
        document.body.classList.remove('no-scroll');
      }

      openBtn.addEventListener('click', openModal);
      closeBtn.addEventListener('click', closeModal);

      overlay.addEventListener('click', function (e) {
        // Close modal if clicking on the backdrop
        if (e.target === overlay) {
          closeModal();
        }
      });

      // Drag logic
      let isDragging = false;
      let dragOffsetX = 0;
      let dragOffsetY = 0;

      // Start dragging
      function startDrag(clientX, clientY) {
        // If the click originated from the close button, ignore drag
        if (event && event.target && event.target.closest('.close-btn')) return;

        const rect = modal.getBoundingClientRect();
        // Offset within the modal where the pointer grabbed it
        dragOffsetX = clientX - rect.left;
        dragOffsetY = clientY - rect.top;

        // Stop centering transform and pin current position in px
        modal.style.transform = 'none';
        modal.style.left = rect.left + 'px';
        modal.style.top = rect.top + 'px';

        isDragging = true;
        header.style.cursor = 'grabbing';
      }

      // Move modal during drag (shared by mouse and touch)
      function moveModal(clientX, clientY) {
        if (!isDragging) return;
        const left = clientX - dragOffsetX;
        const top = clientY - dragOffsetY;

        modal.style.left = left + 'px';
        modal.style.top = top + 'px';
      }

      // End dragging
      function endDrag() {
        isDragging = false;
        header.style.cursor = 'default';
      }

      // Mouse events
      header.addEventListener('mousedown', function (e) {
        // Only respond to left-click
        if (e.button !== 0) return;
        startDrag(e.clientX, e.clientY);

        function onMouseMove(e) {
          moveModal(e.clientX, e.clientY);
        }

        function onMouseUp() {
          endDrag();
          window.removeEventListener('mousemove', onMouseMove);
          window.removeEventListener('mouseup', onMouseUp);
        }

        window.addEventListener('mousemove', onMouseMove);
        window.addEventListener('mouseup', onMouseUp);
      });

      // Touch events
      header.addEventListener('touchstart', function (e) {
        if (!e.touches || e.touches.length === 0) return;
        const tp = e.touches[0];
        startDrag(tp.clientX, tp.clientY);

        function onTouchMove(ev) {
          if (!ev.touches || ev.touches.length === 0) return;
          const t = ev.touches[0];
          moveModal(t.clientX, t.clientY);
          ev.preventDefault(); // prevent scrolling while dragging
        }

        function onTouchEnd() {
          endDrag();
          window.removeEventListener('touchmove', onTouchMove);
          window.removeEventListener('touchend', onTouchEnd);
        }

        window.addEventListener('touchmove', onTouchMove, { passive: false });
        window.addEventListener('touchend', onTouchEnd);
      }, { passive: false });
    })();
  </script>
</body>
</html>
```

How it works:
- The page behind the modal is normal content. When the modal opens, a semi-transparent overlay covers the page and applies a backdrop blur (backdrop-filter: blur(...)).
- The modal is draggable by its header. Clicking and dragging the header moves the modal by updating its left/top in pixels. The initial centering (via transform) is removed when dragging starts to allow precise positioning.
- The overlay closes when you click outside the modal (on the backdrop) or press the close button. The page scroll is optionally disabled while the modal is open.

You can customize blur strength by changing --overlay-blur, modal size, or colors in the CSS. If you need broader browser compatibility, consider conditionally applying a Gaussian blur to a separate background layer instead of backdrop-filter.

      <button id="start" class="btn start" aria-label="Start stopwatch">Start</button>
      <button id="pause" class="btn pause" aria-label="Pause stopwatch">Pause</button>
      <button id="stop" class="btn stop" aria-label="Stop stopwatch (keep current time)">Stop</button>
      <button id="reset" class="btn reset" aria-label="Reset stopwatch to zero">Reset</button>
    </div>

    // State
    let running = false;
    let startTime = 0; // timestamp when timer started or resumed
    let elapsed = 0;   // elapsed time up to last pause/stop

    // DOM
    const display = document.getElementById('display');
    const btnStart = document.getElementById('start');
    const btnPause = document.getElementById('pause');
    const btnStop  = document.getElementById('stop');
    const btnReset = document.getElementById('reset');

    // Animation frame
    let raf = null;

    // Format milliseconds into H:MM:SS.CS or M:SS.CS
    function formatTime(ms) {
      const total = Math.max(0, Math.floor(ms));
      const hours = Math.floor(total / 3600000);
      const minutes = Math.floor((total % 3600000) / 60000);
      const seconds = Math.floor((total % 60000) / 1000);
      const centis = Math.floor((total % 1000) / 10);

      const pad2 = (n) => String(n).padStart(2, '0');
      if (hours > 0) {
        return `${pad2(hours)}:${pad2(minutes)}:${pad2(seconds)}.${pad2(centis)}`;
      } else {
        return `${minutes}:${pad2(seconds)}.${pad2(centis)}`;
      }
    }

    // Update loop (uses requestAnimationFrame for smooth display)
    function update() {
      const value = running ? (Date.now() - startTime) : elapsed;
      display.textContent = formatTime(value);
      raf = requestAnimationFrame(update);
    }

    // Controls
    function start() {
      if (!running) {
        startTime = Date.now() - elapsed;
        running = true;
        updateUI();
      }
    }

    function pause() {
      if (running) {
        elapsed = Date.now() - startTime;
        running = false;
        updateUI();
      }
    }

    // Stop: stops the timer but keeps the current elapsed visible
    function stop() {
      if (running) {
        elapsed = Date.now() - startTime;
        running = false;
        updateUI();
      } else {
        // If already stopped, keep current elapsed visible
      }
    }

    // Reset: zeroes elapsed and resets timer base
    function reset() {
      elapsed = 0;
      if (running) {
        startTime = Date.now(); // reset base so time starts from zero
      } else {
        // If not running, ensure display shows zero
        display.textContent = formatTime(0);
      }
      updateUI();
    }

    function updateUI() {
      // Optional: disable/enable buttons for better UX
      btnStart.disabled = running;
      btnPause.disabled = !running;
      // Stop and Reset are always available in this simple UI
    }

    // Attach events
    btnStart.addEventListener('click', start);
    btnPause.addEventListener('click', pause);
    btnStop.addEventListener('click', stop);
    btnReset.addEventListener('click', reset);

    // Initialize
    updateUI();
    update(); // start the loop
  </script>
</body>
</html>

Notes:
