Notes on accessibility and security

Accessibility improvements
- Labels tied to inputs: Each input has a corresponding label with a for attribute and the input has a matching id. This ensures screen readers announce the control clearly and describe its purpose.
- ARIA description through aria-describedby: Each input has aria-describedby pointing to help text that explains requirements or usage. Screen readers will read the help text in addition to the label, giving users more context.
- Semantic, native controls: Using input types text, email, password, and range provides appropriate semantics and default accessibility support. Mobile keyboards adapt to the input type (e.g., email keyboard, password masking).
- Validation messaging using HTML5: Required, minlength, maxlength, pattern, and type="email" give immediate, built-in feedback without needing custom scripts. This reduces the risk of missing or inconsistent validation for assistive tech users.
- Range accessibility: The range input exposes min, max, and step (and ARIA values) so assistive technologies can convey the current value and the allowed range. The visible output (ratingValue) is updated in real time for clarity.
- Autocomplete hints: Autocomplete attributes (name, email, new-password) help users reuse stored credentials securely and reduce keystrokes, especially for assistive tech users.

Security improvements
- Proper input types: Using type="email" ensures basic format validation, reducing malformed data reaching the server. type="password" keeps input masked, protecting sensitive data from onlookers.
- Password handling: autocomplete="new-password" prevents password managers from filling in old passwords in this field, which supports better security hygiene when creating a new password.
- Client-side validation compliments server checks: HTML5 attributes provide immediate feedback and reduce unnecessary server load. They also help prevent obviously invalid data from being submitted, improving overall input hygiene.
- Controlled data constraints: Minlength, maxlength, and pattern help enforce acceptable formats (e.g., password length, name characters) before data leaves the client, reducing some classes of malformed input.

Performance and UX notes
- Native validation messages from the browser are consistent across platforms and accessible to assistive technologies without additional code.
- If you need custom error messaging, you can use the Constraint Validation API to read validity states and present accessible messages via aria-live regions.

1) HTTP/2 caching headers (server-side)

Goal: serve assets with long-term caching when hashed filenames are used, while not caching HTML. Use HTTP/2 (via a Node server with TLS). This example uses Express with spdy (HTTP/2) so you don’t have to wire http2 directly.

File: server.js

const express = require('express');
const spdy = require('spdy');
const fs = require('fs');
const path = require('path');

const app = express();
const ONE_YEAR = 31536000; // seconds

// Caching policy
function setCacheHeaders(req, res, next) {
  // Do not cache HTML pages
  const isHTML = req.path === '/' || req.path.endsWith('.html');
  if (isHTML) {
    res.setHeader('Cache-Control', 'no-store');
  } else {
    // Hash-named assets (e.g., main.abc123.js) can be cached for a year
    // "immutable" indicates the asset won't change unless the URL changes
    res.setHeader('Cache-Control', `public, max-age=${ONE_YEAR}, immutable`);
  }
  next();
}

app.use(setCacheHeaders);

// Serve static assets (your built React app)
app.use('/', express.static(path.resolve(__dirname, 'dist'), { index: false }));

// Optional: preload hints can be added via Link headers (dynamic in real apps)
app.use((req, res, next) => {
  // Example: res.setHeader('Link', '</static/js/main.abc123.js>; rel=preload; as=script');
  next();
});

// TLS options (replace with your certs)
const options = {
  key: fs.readFileSync(path.resolve(__dirname, 'ssl', 'server.key')),
  cert: fs.readFileSync(path.resolve(__dirname, 'ssl', 'server.crt')),
};

spdy.createServer(options, app).listen(8443, (err) => {
  if (err) throw err;
  console.log('HTTP/2 server with caching headers listening on https://localhost:8443');
});

Notes and tips:
- Use hashed filenames for your JS/CSS assets (e.g., main.[hash].js). This makes the "immutable" caching safe.
- HTML and dynamic content should typically have short or no caching (no-store or no-cache).
- In production, you may terminate TLS at a reverse proxy (e.g., NGINX) and still push HTTP/2 with proper headers from your app.
- You can add Link/header-based preloads or preconnect hints as needed (e.g., preload your main bundles).

2) Code splitting (dynamic imports) in a React app

Goal: split code by route or feature to enable lazy loading and smaller initial bundles.

Files (React app with React Router v6 and dynamic imports)

src/App.jsx

import React, { Suspense, lazy } from 'react';
import { BrowserRouter as Router, Routes, Route, Link } from 'react-router-dom';

// Lazy-load pages (code-splitting)
const Home = lazy(() => import('./pages/Home'));
const About = lazy(() => import('./pages/About'));
const Dashboard = lazy(() => import('./pages/Dashboard'));

export default function App() {
  return (
    <Router>
      <nav>
        <Link to="/">Home</Link> |{' '}
        <Link to="/about">About</Link> |{' '}
        <Link to="/dashboard">Dashboard</Link>
      </nav>

      {/* Suspense shows fallback until the lazy component loads */}
      <Suspense fallback={<div>Loading...</div>}>
        <Routes>
          <Route path="/" element={<Home />} />
          <Route path="/about" element={<About />} />
          <Route path="/dashboard" element={<Dashboard />} />
        </Routes>
      </Suspense>
    </Router>
  );
}

src/pages/Home.jsx, About.jsx, Dashboard.jsx

3) Web Workers for background processing

Goal: move heavy computations off the main thread.

Option A: classic (non-module) worker file

File: src/workers/heavyWorker.js

self.onmessage = function(e) {
  const { iterations } = e.data;
  // Simulated heavy work
  let sum = 0;
  for (let i = 0; i < iterations; i++) {
    sum += Math.sqrt(i) * Math.sin(i);
  }
  self.postMessage({ result: sum });
};

Option B: module worker (more modern; bundlers like Vite/Webpack support this)

File: src/workers/heavyWorker.mjs
self.onmessage = function(e) {
  const { iterations } = e.data;
  let sum = 0;
  for (let i = 0; i < iterations; i++) {
    sum += Math.log(i + 1);
  }
  self.postMessage({ result: sum });
};

Main thread usage (React component)

src/components/HeavyComputation.jsx

import React, { useEffect, useRef, useState } from 'react';

export default function HeavyComputation({ iterations }) {
  const [result, setResult] = useState(null);
  const workerRef = useRef(null);

  useEffect(() => {
    // For classic worker (no module)
    // const w = new Worker('/path/to/heavyWorker.js');
    // w.onmessage = (e) => setResult(e.data.result);
    // w.postMessage({ iterations });

    // For module worker (preferred if your bundler supports it)
    const w = new Worker(new URL('./../workers/heavyWorker.mjs', import.meta.url), { type: 'module' });
    w.onmessage = (e) => setResult(e.data.result);
    w.onerror = (err) => console.error('Worker error:', err);
    w.postMessage({ iterations });

    workerRef.current = w;
    return () => w.terminate();
  }, [iterations]);

  return (
    <div>
      <div>Heavy computation result: {result ?? 'computing...'}</div>
    </div>
  );
}

Notes and tips:
- Use web workers when tasks are CPU-bound to keep UI responsive.
- If you have many tasks, consider a pool of workers or a library like workerize or Comlink to simplify communication.
- When using module workers, your bundler must support them (e.g., Vite/Webpack with appropriate loader/config).

Putting it all together

- HTTP/2 with caching headers: set up a TLS-enabled HTTP/2 server (Express + spdy in example) and return long Cache-Control headers for static assets with hashed names, and short/none for HTML.
- React code-splitting: use React.lazy and Suspense (and, if you want, route-based splitting with react-router) to dynamically import components.
- Web Workers: offload heavy computations to a worker file; create and communicate via postMessage, ideally using a module worker for modern tooling.

It's essential to highlight the choice between utility functions and class-based approaches based on how the duplication occurs, keeping it straightforward and informative!**Refactoring mixins into utility functions and classes**

I’m planning to create a clear guide on refactoring mixins by summarizing different approaches. First, I’ll list the methods to tackle duplication, such as using shared utility functions and defining a base class. 

Next, I want to show specific code examples demonstrating before and after scenarios. For instance, I’ll illustrate how to replace duplicate formatting functions and error handling with utility imports and how to refactor common methods into a base class, making the code cleaner and more maintainable.</think> Here are practical, copy-pasteable examples showing how to remove duplicated logic from a JavaScript mixin pattern by using ES6 utilities or base classes. The goal is to keep mixins focused while factoring out shared behavior so you don’t replicate code across mixins.

Idea at a glance
- If you’re duplicating small helpers (like formatDate, log formatting, error handling) in multiple mixins, move those helpers into a shared utility module and have mixins call into it.
- If you’re duplicating lifecycle or common behavior across mixins, consider a small base class (or composition with small helper classes) to hold that shared logic, and have concrete classes extend that base.
- In some cases, you’ll combine both: use utility modules for helpers and a base class for shared behavior, then use pure ES6 classes and simple mixin factories for composition.

Example 1: Duplicated helper (formatDate) across two mixins
Before (duplicated formatDate in two mixins)

```js
// mixins.js
const DataFetcher = (Base) => class extends Base {
  fetch() {
    return fetch(this.url)
      .then(res => res.json())
      .then(data => { this.data = data; })
      .catch(err => this.handleError(err));
  }

  // duplicated logic
  formatDate(date) {
    const t = new Date(date).toISOString();
    return t;
  }
};

const DataSaver = (Base) => class extends Base {
  save() {
    try {
      localStorage.setItem(this.key, JSON.stringify(this.data));
    } catch (err) {
      this.handleError(err);
    }
  }

  // duplicated logic
  formatDate(date) {
    const t = new Date(date).toISOString();
    return t;
  }
};

// usage
class MyView extends DataSaver(DataFetcher(class {})) {
  constructor() {
    super();
    this.url = '/api/user';
    this.key = 'user';
  }
}
```

After (factor the shared helper into a utility module and reuse it)

```js
// dateUtils.js
export function formatDate(date) {
  return new Date(date).toISOString();
}
```

```js
// mixins.js
import { formatDate } from './dateUtils.js';

const DataFetcher = (Base) => class extends Base {
  fetch() {
    return fetch(this.url)
      .then(res => res.json())
      .then(data => { this.data = data; })
      .catch(err => this.handleError(err));
  }

  // use the shared utility
  formatDate(date) {
    return formatDate(date);
  }
};

const DataSaver = (Base) => class extends Base {
  save() {
    try {
      localStorage.setItem(this.key, JSON.stringify(this.data));
    } catch (err) {
      this.handleError(err);
    }
  }

  // use the shared utility
  formatDate(date) {
    return formatDate(date);
  }
};

// usage

  }
}
```

Notes
- The duplicated formatDate logic is now centralized in dateUtils.js. If formatting needs change, you update one place.
- The mixins still compose behavior; they just don’t duplicate the same helper logic anymore.

Example 3: Refactor toward ES6 classes / composition instead of duplicating mixins
Before (two independent mixins with overlapping responsibilities)

```js
// mixins.js
const LoggerMixin = (Base) => class extends Base {
  log(msg) {
    console.log(`[Logger] ${new Date().toISOString()} - ${msg}`);
  }
};

const TimestampMixin = (Base) => class extends Base {
  stamp() {
    return new Date().toISOString();
  }
};

class Widget {}

class UserWidget extends LoggerMixin(TimestampMixin(Widget)) {
  render() {
    this.log('rendering user widget');
    // ...
  }
  getStamp() {
    return this.stamp();
  }
}
```

After (move shared concerns to focused, reusable base/classes and/or use composition)

Option 1: base class for shared concerns
```js
class BaseModel {
  log(msg) {
    console.log(`[${this.constructor.name}] ${msg}`);
  }
  static formatDate(d) {
    return new Date(d).toISOString();
  }
}

class UserWidget extends BaseModel {
  constructor() { super(); /* ... */ }
  render() {
    this.log('rendering user widget');
    // ...
  }
  getStamp() {
    return BaseModel.formatDate(Date.now());
  }
}
```

Option 2: simple composition with small helper classes (instead of multiple mixins)
```js
class Logger {
  log(msg) { console.log(`[Logger] ${msg}`); }
}
class Timestamp {
  stamp() { return new Date().toISOString(); }
}

class UserWidget {
  constructor() {
    Object.assign(this, new Logger(), new Timestamp());
  }
  render() {
    this.log('rendering user widget');
    // ...
  }
  getStamp() {
    return this.stamp();
  }
}
```

Notes
- When you find yourself piling several mixins on top of each other just to share a few small bits of logic, consider replacing with an ES6 class (base or single-purpose) or with composition (have the class own small helper objects and delegate to them). This reduces method-name collisions and makes the control flow clearer.

Best-practice tips
- Start with the source of truth: if you’re duplicating the same helper in multiple mixins, extract it to a utility module and import from there.
- If multiple mixins share lifecycle or state management, consider a base class or a small set of composable helper classes that your final class can use via delegation.
- Favor named utilities over “hidden” copies of logic inside mixins. This improves testability and readability.
- Be mindful of method resolution order and potential name collisions when layering mixins. Using utilities or a base class helps avoid subtle bugs.

Notes:
- XOR is not secure encryption; this is a toy example to demonstrate a WASM wrapper around a performance-critical loop. For real encryption, use a proven library (e.g., AES-GCM via WebCrypto).
- The WASM in this example is designed to be easy to understand and modify. If you want to run it in a browser without building, you’ll either:

  - Precompile the WASM binary and load it directly (see the “precompiled WASM” path below).

1) The WASM module (as WAT text)
This is a tiny module that supports a simple heap allocator and a crypt function that XORs input with a key and writes to output.

WAT (module.wat)
(Note: This is the text form. You need to compile it to binary WASM before loading in a real environment, or use an in-browser WAT->WASM tool such as WABT.)

; WebAssembly Text Format (WAT)
(module
  ;; One-page memory (64KiB)
  (memory (export "memory") 1)

  ;; Simple heap pointer starting at 1024
  (global $heap_ptr (mut i32) (i32.const 1024))

  ;; Allocate 'size' bytes and return old pointer
  (func (export "alloc") (param $size i32) (result i32)
    (local $addr i32)
    (global.get $heap_ptr)       ;; old heap_ptr
    (local.set $addr)

    (local.get $addr)
    (local.get $size)
    (i32.add)
    (global.set $heap_ptr)         ;; heap_ptr += size

    (local.get $addr)               ;; return old address
  )

  ;; Encrypt: crypt(in_ptr, out_ptr, len, key)
  ;; out[i] = in[i] ^ (key & 0xFF)
  (func (export "crypt")
    (param $in_ptr i32)  (param $out_ptr i32)
    (param $len i32)     (param $key i32)
    (local $i i32)

    (local.set $i (i32.const 0))

    (block $done
      (loop $loop
        (br_if $done (i32.ge_u (local.get $i) (local.get $len)))

        ;; load in[i]
        (i32.load8_u (i32.add (local.get $in_ptr) (local.get $i)))
        ;; key & 0xff
        (local.get $key)
        (i32.const 0xff)
        (i32.and)
        ;; xor
        (i32.xor)

        ;; compute address out_ptr + i (push address)
        (local.get $out_ptr)
        (local.get $i)
        (i32.add)
        ;; store: value is the result below on the stack; address is top
        (i32.store8)

        ;; i++
        (local.set $i (i32.add (local.get $i) (i32.const 1)))
        (br $loop)
      )
    )
  )
)

2) JavaScript wrapper (dynamic WASM load with optional in-browser WAT compilation)
This wrapper demonstrates two ways to load the WASM:
- Precompiled WASM binary (base64) path (fast to load in production)
- In-browser WAT-to-WASM path using a tool like WABT (for experimentation)

- Pure-JS XOR for comparison
- Tiny benchmark

Code (js wrapper)
- This example is written to run in Node.js or modern browsers.

Paste this into a single JS file and run with Node (node yourfile.js) or paste into a browser console after including a WABT tool if you want to compile WAT in-browser.

"use strict";

async function createWasmCrypto() {
  // 1) Pick one path: precompiled WASM, or WAT-to-WASM (requires wabt.js)
  // Path A: Precompiled WASM (base64-encoded)
  // You can replace this blob with your own compiled WebAssembly binary.
  const wasmBase64 = null; // set to a base64 string if you have a precompiled module
  // Path B: In-browser WAT -> WASM (requires wabt.js)
  const watSource = `(module
    (memory (export "memory") 1)
    (global $heap_ptr (mut i32) (i32.const 1024))
    (func (export "alloc") (param $size i32) (result i32)
      (local $addr i32)
      (global.get $heap_ptr)
      (local.set $addr)
      (local.get $addr)
      (local.get $size)
      (i32.add)
      (global.set $heap_ptr)
      (local.get $addr)
    )
    (func (export "crypt")
      (param $in_ptr i32) (param $out_ptr i32)
      (param $len i32) (param $key i32)
      (local $i i32)
      (local.set $i (i32.const 0))
      (block $done
        (loop $loop
          (br_if $done (i32.ge_u (local.get $i) (local.get $len)))
          ;; val = in_ptr[i]
          (i32.load8_u (i32.add (local.get $in_ptr) (local.get $i)))
          ;; key' = key & 0xff
          (local.get $key) (i32.const 0xff) (i32.and)
          ;; val ^ key'
          (i32.xor)
          ;; address = out_ptr + i
          (local.get $out_ptr) (local.get $i) (i32.add)
          ;; store
          (i32.store8)
          (local.set $i (i32.add (local.get $i) (i32.const 1)))
          (br $loop)
        )
      )
    )
  )`;

  // Helper: JS XOR for comparison
  function encryptJS(data, key) {
    const k = key & 0xff;
    const out = new Uint8Array(data.length);
    for (let i = 0; i < data.length; i++) {
      out[i] = data[i] ^ k;
    }
    return out;
  }

  // 2) Instantiate WASM
  let wasmInstance;
  if (wasmBase64) {
    // Path A: load precompiled wasm binary
    const bytes = Uint8Array.from(atob(wasmBase64), c => c.charCodeAt(0));
    const mod = await WebAssembly.instantiate(bytes.buffer, {});
    wasmInstance = mod.instance;
  } else {
    // Path B: compile WAT to WASM at runtime (requires wabt.js)
    // You can load wabt.js and use it like:
    // const wabt = await WabtModule(); // load from a script tag or module
    // const mod = wabt.parseWat("module.wat", watSource);
    // const binary = mod.toBinary({ write_debug_names: true }).buffer;
    // const mod2 = await WebAssembly.instantiate(binary, {});
    // wasmInstance = mod2.instance;

    // Minimal fallback if you can't import wabt.js here:
    throw new Error("No precompiled WASM available and WAT->WASM path requires wabt.js in-browser setup.");
  }

  // 3) Create wrappers around exports
  const memory = wasmInstance.exports.memory;
  const alloc = wasmInstance.exports.alloc;
  const crypt = wasmInstance.exports.crypt;

  // Simple memory views helper
  function ensureMemory(len) {
    // Ensure there is enough space: allocate length bytes for input and output each
    // We'll allocate two blocks of 'len' bytes
    // This is a simple approach; a more robust approach would maintain a small allocator for reuse.
    const needed = len * 2;
    const currentBytes = memory.buffer.byteLength;
    if (currentBytes < 1024 + needed) {
      // Grow memory if needed; WebAssembly memory growth requires pages (64KiB each)
      const pagesNeeded = Math.ceil((1024 + needed - currentBytes) / 65536);
      memory.grow(pagesNeeded);
    }
  }

  // Public API
  return {
    encrypt: function(input, key) {
      // Input: Uint8Array
      // Output: new Uint8Array with encrypted bytes
      const len = input.byteLength;
      ensureMemory(len);

      // Allocate two blocks in WASM memory
      const inPtr = alloc(len);
      const outPtr = alloc(len);

      // Copy input into WASM memory
      const mem = new Uint8Array(memory.buffer);
      mem.set(input, inPtr);

      // Run crypt(in_ptr, out_ptr, len, key)
      crypt(inPtr, outPtr, len, key);

      // Copy result back to JS
      const result = new Uint8Array(memory.buffer.slice(outPtr, outPtr + len));
      return result;
    },
    encryptJS: function(input, key) {
      return encryptJS(input, key);
    }
  };
}

// 4) Example usage and tiny benchmark
(async () => {
  try {
    const wasmCrypto = await createWasmCrypto();
    // Example plaintext
    const text = "The quick brown fox jumps over the lazy dog. Encrypt me!";
    const encoder = new TextEncoder();
    const data = encoder.encode(text);
    const key = 0x5A; // 90

    // JS baseline
    console.time("JS XOR");
    const jsOut = wasmCrypto.encryptJS(data, key);
    console.timeEnd("JS XOR");

    // WASM path
    console.time("WASM XOR");
    const wasmOut = wasmCrypto.encrypt(data, key);
    console.timeEnd("WASM XOR");

    // Simple sanity check
    console.log("JS out:", Array.from(jsOut).slice(0, 16));
    console.log("WASM out:", Array.from(wasmOut).slice(0, 16));
  } catch (e) {
    console.error("Error setting up WASM crypto:", e);
  }
})();

What to customize and how to run
- If you already have a precompiled WASM binary:
  - Put the base64 of the binary into wasmBase64 in the code.
  - The wrapper will instantiate the module directly (Path A).
- If you want to compile WAT to WASM in-browser (Path B):
  - Load wabt.js (the WABT toolkit) in your page.
  - Replace the Path B comment with real in-browser compilation code, e.g.:
    - const wabt = await WabtModule();
    - const mod = wabt.parseWat("module.wat", watSource);
    - const binary = mod.toBinary({ write_debug_names: true }).buffer;
    - const mod2 = await WebAssembly.instantiate(binary, {});
    - wasmInstance = mod2.instance;
  - Then run as usual.

Performance notes
- In many practical cases, WebAssembly outperforms plain JavaScript for byte-wise loops due to near-native execution speed and better optimization in the engine.
- The XOR operation is extremely lightweight; the main gains come when encrypting large payloads or many chunks in a loop.
- For real-world encryption needs, prefer a proven algorithm in a secure mode (e.g., AES-GCM) and consider using the Web Crypto API for hardware-accelerated primitives. WASM can be used for other performance-critical parts or custom nonces/cryptographic transforms where Web Crypto isn’t suitable.

It also includes a small registration script to register the service worker.

What this does
- On install: pre-caches a list of assets (startup caching).
- On fetch: serves from cache when possible (offline-ready) and starts a background revalidation against the server.
- Revalidation: if the cached response has an ETag, the SW asks the server with If-None-Match. If the server says the resource changed (200), the cache is updated. If not changed (304 or no update), nothing is changed.
- Server requirement for true validation: the server must expose ETag (and optionally Last-Modified) so the SW can use conditional requests. If ETag isn’t available, it falls back to a non-conditional fetch to refresh when possible.

Files you’ll need

1) Registration script (e.g., register-sw.js)
- Register the service worker when the page loads.

```javascript
// register-sw.js
if ('serviceWorker' in navigator) {
  window.addEventListener('load', () => {
    navigator.serviceWorker.register('/sw.js')
      .then(reg => {
        console.log('Service Worker registered with scope:', reg.scope);
      })
      .catch(err => {
        console.error('Service Worker registration failed:', err);
      });
  });
}
```

2) Service worker (sw.js)
- Caches assets at startup and validates them against the server on subsequent requests.

```javascript
// sw.js

// Assets to cache at startup
const CACHE_NAME = 'site-cache-v1';
const ASSETS = [
  '/',                 // root
  '/index.html',
  '/styles.css',
  '/scripts/main.js',
  '/offline.html',
  '/images/logo.png'
];

// Install: pre-cache assets (startup caching)
self.addEventListener('install', (event) => {
  event.waitUntil(
    caches.open(CACHE_NAME)
      .then((cache) => cache.addAll(ASSETS))
      .then(() => self.skipWaiting())
  );
});

// Activate: clean up old caches if needed
self.addEventListener('activate', (event) => {
  const allowed = [CACHE_NAME];
  event.waitUntil(
    caches.keys().then((keys) => {
      return Promise.all(
        keys.filter((k) => !allowed.includes(k)).map((k) => caches.delete(k))
      );
    }).then(() => self.clients.claim())
  );
});

// Helper: update cache with server validation (ETag-based if available)
async function revalidateWithServer(request) {
  try {
    const cachedResponse = await caches.match(request);
    if (!cachedResponse) {
      return;
    }

    // Try to revalidate using If-None-Match if we have an ETag
    const etag = cachedResponse.headers.get('ETag');
    if (etag) {
      // Build a conditional request with If-None-Match
      const headers = new Headers(request.headers);
      headers.set('If-None-Match', etag);
      const conditionalRequest = new Request(request, {
        headers: headers
      });

      const serverResp = await fetch(conditionalRequest);

      if (serverResp && serverResp.status === 200) {
        // Resource updated on server; refresh cache
        const cache = await caches.open(CACHE_NAME);
        await cache.put(request, serverResp.clone());
      }
      // If 304 Not Modified, do nothing (cache is still fresh)
      return;
    }

    // Fallback: try a normal fetch if no ETag available
    const resp = await fetch(request);
    if (resp && resp.ok) {
      const cache = await caches.open(CACHE_NAME);
      await cache.put(request, resp.clone());
    }
  } catch (e) {
    // Ignore network/validation errors to avoid failing the fetch
  }
}

// Fetch: serve from cache, but also validate in background
self.addEventListener('fetch', (event) => {
  // Only handle GET requests for caching strategy
  if (event.request.method !== 'GET') {
    return;
  }

  event.respondWith(
    (async () => {
      const cached = await caches.match(event.request);
      // Start a background revalidation if we have a cached response
      if (cached) {
        event.waitUntil(revalidateWithServer(event.request));
        return cached;
      }

      // If not cached, fetch from network and cache it
      try {
        const networkResponse = await fetch(event.request);
        if (networkResponse && networkResponse.ok) {
          const cache = await caches.open(CACHE_NAME);
          await cache.put(event.request, networkResponse.clone());
        }
        return networkResponse;
      } catch (e) {
        // Optional: return a fallback (offline) response if available
        const offline = await caches.match('/offline.html');
        return offline || new Response('Offline', { status: 503, statusText: 'Offline' });
      }
    })()
  );
});
```

Notes and caveats
- ETag exposure: For the revalidation path to work as shown, your server must expose the ETag header via CORS if assets are cross-origin. You may need to configure CORS headers like Access-Control-Expose-Headers: ETag on the server side.
- Fallbacks: If you don’t have ETag support, the code falls back to a normal fetch to refresh assets when possible.
- Offline fallback: The example includes offline.html as a fallback; ensure you have such a file if you want a friendly offline page.
- Cache versioning: Update CACHE_NAME (e.g., 'site-cache-v2') when you change assets so old caches are replaced.
- Security: Service workers run on HTTPS or localhost. Ensure your app is served securely during development and production.

How to use
- Place register-sw.js in your web root and include it in your HTML (e.g., in index.html’s script tag or load it from your main JS):
  - <script src="/register-sw.js"></script>
- Ensure sw.js is at the root as referenced by the registration path (adjust paths accordingly for your project).
- On first load, the service worker caches the assets listed in ASSETS.
- On subsequent visits, requests are served from the cache while the service worker validates against the server in the background, updating the cache if the server indicates changes via ETag.
